questions.prompt: A sorted array and a target are given. Find two values that sum to the target using O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Which pattern fits?
options: Two Pointers
Sliding Window
Hash Map lookup
Binary Search per element
questions.explanation: Start one pointer at each end. If the sum is too small move the left pointer right, if too large move the right pointer left; each step discards one candidate, so it is O(n) time and O(1) space. A hash map is also O(n) time but needs O(n) space, and binary search per element is O(n log n).

questions.prompt: Return an array where out[i] is the product of every element except nums[i], without using division, in O(n) time. Which pattern fits?
options: Prefix/Suffix Pass
Sliding Window
Monotonic Stack
Two Pointers
questions.explanation: One left-to-right pass stores the product of everything before each index, then a right-to-left pass multiplies in the product of everything after it. Two passes give O(n) time, and the output array is the only extra space (O(1) auxiliary).

questions.prompt: What are the worst-case time and extra space of this function for a list of n integers?
options: O(n) time, O(n) space
O(n) time, O(1) space
O(n²) time, O(n) space
O(n log n) time, O(1) space
questions.explanation: Set membership and insertion are O(1) on average, so the loop is O(n). When all values are distinct the set grows to n elements, so extra space is O(n). Sorting first would give O(n log n) time but O(1) extra space, which is a different trade-off.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
out = [1] * len(nums)
for i in range(1, len(nums)):
    out[i] = out[i - 1] * nums[i - 1]
print(out)
questions.explanation: out[i] is the product of nums[0..i-1]: out[1]=1, out[2]=1*2=2, out[3]=2*3=6. This is the prefix half of Product of Array Except Self. Time O(n), space O(n) for out.

questions.prompt: This function should rotate nums right by k steps in place, but it gives a wrong result for some inputs (for example nums=[1,2,3], k=4). What is the bug?
questions.code:
def rotate(nums, k):
    nums[:] = nums[-k:] + nums[:-k]
options: k is not reduced with k %= len(nums), so k larger than the length does nothing
The slice assignment builds a new list instead of changing nums in place
nums[-k:] raises IndexError when k is 0
It should be nums[k:] + nums[:k]
questions.explanation: When k > len(nums), nums[-k:] is the whole list and nums[:-k] is empty, so the list is unchanged instead of rotating by k % n. Add k %= len(nums) first (and guard against an empty list). The slice assignment nums[:] = ... does mutate in place, and slicing never raises IndexError. Time O(n), space O(n) for the temporary list; the three-reversal trick gets O(1) extra space.

questions.prompt: You must set an entire row and column to 0 whenever a matrix cell is 0, modifying the m×n matrix in place. Which approach achieves O(1) extra space?
options: Use the first row and first column as markers, tracking separately whether they themselves need zeroing
Store the zero rows and zero columns in two sets, then zero them
Copy the matrix and fill zeros into the copy
Zero rows and columns immediately while scanning
questions.explanation: Reuse the first row and column as flag storage (after recording two booleans for whether they originally contained a zero), then zero the interior from those flags and finally the first row and column if needed. Time O(m·n), space O(1). Sets cost O(m+n), a copy costs O(m·n), and zeroing while scanning corrupts cells you have not read yet.

questions.prompt: Remove every occurrence of a given value from an array in place, keeping the order of the other elements, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Which technique fits?
options: Sliding Window over the longest run without the value
Monotonic Stack that pops the value
Read/Write Pointer (one pointer scans, one marks where the next kept element goes)
Hash Set of the values already seen
questions.explanation: A scanning pointer reads each element and a second pointer writes it forward only when it is kept, so everything stays in one pass with no extra array. Time O(n), space O(1). A hash set solves a different problem (duplicates), and a stack or window adds structure this task does not need.

questions.prompt: Rotate an n×n matrix 90 degrees clockwise in place, with O(1) extra space. Which pattern fits?
options: Transpose the matrix, then reverse each row
Reverse each row, then reverse each column
Boundary-shrinking spiral copying into a new matrix
Copy into a new matrix using result[c][n-1-r] = m[r][c]
questions.explanation: Rotating clockwise equals a transpose (swap m[r][c] with m[c][r] for c > r) followed by reversing every row. Both steps are in place: time O(n²), space O(1). Reversing rows then columns is a 180° rotation, and the copy approach uses O(n²) extra space.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of this function for a positive integer n?
options: O(n)
O(√n)
O(n log n)
O(log n)
questions.explanation: i doubles each iteration (1, 2, 4, 8, ...), so the loop stops after about log₂ n iterations. A loop that multiplies or divides its variable by a constant factor is logarithmic. Space is O(1).

questions.prompt: What are the time and extra space of this function for a list of n integers?
options: O(n²) time, O(1) space
O(n²) time, O(n²) space
O(n) time, O(n) space
O(n log n) time, O(n²) space
questions.explanation: The nested loops run (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 = n(n-1)/2 times, which is O(n²). Each iteration appends one pair, so the result list also holds n(n-1)/2 tuples: O(n²) space. The result is output, but it is still memory the function allocates.

questions.prompt: Assume every `+=` on a string copies the whole string built so far. Worst-case time to concatenate n words of length k each with this loop?
options: O(n · k)
O(n · k²)
O(n log n · k)
O(n² · k)
questions.explanation: After i words the string has i·k characters, and `s += w` copies all of them. The total copying is k·(1 + 2 + ... + n) = k·n(n+1)/2, which is O(n²·k). Collecting the words in a list and calling `''.join(words)` does one pass over n·k characters: O(n·k) time, O(n·k) space. CPython sometimes resizes in place as an optimization, but you should not rely on it.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of this function for a positive integer n?
options: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(n²)
O(log n)
questions.explanation: The outer loop runs about log₂ n times, but the inner loop shrinks each time: n + n/2 + n/4 + ... < 2n. A geometric series is dominated by its first term, so the total is O(n), not O(n log n). Space is O(1).

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: `[[0] * 3] * 2` repeats a reference to the same inner list, so both rows are one object and changing grid[0][1] shows up in grid[1][1]. Build grids with `[[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)]`. Time O(m·n) to build, space O(m·n).

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Slice assignment replaces the whole slice nums[1:4] (indices 1, 2, 3) with the right-hand sequence, and the list shrinks or grows to fit. Three elements were replaced by one. The cost is O(n) because the tail shifts.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
s = "abc"
t = s
s += "d"
print(t, s)
options: abcd abcd
abc abcd
abc abc
abcd abc
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable, so `s += "d"` builds a new string and rebinds s. t still points to the old "abc". The same statement on a list (`+=`) would mutate in place and change t as well.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: `zip(*m)` yields the columns as tuples: (1, 4), (2, 5), (3, 6). Reversing each tuple with [::-1] gives another tuple, so the rows of the clockwise rotation are tuples, printed with parentheses. Wrap each in list() if you need lists. Time O(m·n), space O(m·n).

questions.prompt: This backward merge of nums2 into nums1 (which has m values followed by n spare slots) loses an element. What is the bug?
options: i should start at m instead of m - 1
k should start at m + n instead of m + n - 1
The loop condition should be `while j >= 0`; `j > 0` never copies nums2[0]
The comparison should be >= instead of >
questions.explanation: The loop must run until every element of nums2 is placed, including index 0. With `j > 0` it stops with nums2[0] still unplaced, so for nums1=[1,2,3,0,0,0], nums2=[2,5,6] the 2 from nums2 is never copied. Writing from the back is what makes it O(1) space; the other start indices shown are the correct ones. Time O(m + n), space O(1).

questions.prompt: This function should return the longest common prefix of the strings, but returns "low" for ["low", "flower"] (the answer is ""). What is the bug?
options: `in` tests for any substring; it should be `not s.startswith(prefix)`
prefix should be trimmed from the front, not the back
strs[1:] skips the last string
prefix should start as min(strs) instead of strs[0]
questions.explanation: `prefix not in s` is satisfied by a substring anywhere in s, so "low" is accepted because it appears inside "flower", although it is not a prefix of it. A prefix test is `s.startswith(prefix)`. With the fix, each string shortens prefix at most len(prefix) times: O(S) time where S is the total number of characters, O(1) extra space.

questions.prompt: This function should add one to a number stored as a list of digits, but plus_one([9, 9]) returns [0, 0] instead of [1, 0, 0]. What is missing?
options: The loop must run left to right so the carry moves forward
The test should be `d[i] <= 9`
A final `return [1] + d` for the case where every digit was 9
d[i] = 0 should be placed before the if
questions.explanation: Carries propagate from the least significant digit, so scanning right to left is correct. When every digit is 9 the loop ends with all zeros and a carry left over, which needs a new leading 1. Time O(n), space O(1) except for the rare extra digit (O(n) when the list is rebuilt).

questions.prompt: Given daily stock prices, return the maximum profit from one buy followed by a later sell (0 if none). Which plan is best?
options: One pass: keep the lowest price so far and the best profit if you sold today
Sort the prices and return the largest minus the smallest
Compare every pair (i, j) with i < j and keep the best
Build a prefix-sum array and take its maximum
questions.explanation: Selling on day j is best paired with the cheapest earlier day, so track min_price as you scan and update best = max(best, price - min_price). Time O(n), space O(1). Sorting destroys the order (buy must come before sell), and the pair scan is O(n²).

questions.prompt: nums1 holds m sorted values followed by n empty slots, and nums2 holds n sorted values. Merge them into nums1 in O(m + n) time and O(1) extra space. Which plan works?
options: Merge from the front with two pointers, writing into nums1 as you go
Copy nums2 into the spare slots and call nums1.sort()
Insert each nums2 value into nums1 with list.insert
Fill nums1 from the back with three pointers, always placing the larger of the two current tails
questions.explanation: Writing from the back never overwrites an unread nums1 value because the empty slots are at the end. A front merge overwrites values that have not been read yet. Copy + sort is O((m+n) log(m+n)) and `insert` shifts elements, giving O(m·n) in the worst case. Back-fill is O(m + n) time, O(1) space.

questions.prompt: Return the elements of an m×n matrix in spiral order in O(m·n) time and O(1) extra space beyond the output. Which plan works?
options: Keep a visited matrix and turn right whenever the next cell is out of bounds or visited
Keep top, bottom, left and right boundaries; sweep each side and shrink the boundary, rechecking top <= bottom and left <= right between sweeps
Recursively slice off the outer ring into a new sub-matrix
Transpose the matrix and then reverse each row
questions.explanation: Four shrinking boundaries visit every cell exactly once with a handful of integers: time O(m·n), space O(1). A visited matrix costs O(m·n) extra space, recursive slicing copies the interior on every level, and transpose + reverse rotates the matrix rather than walking it. The recheck between sweeps prevents repeating a row or column when the matrix is a single row or column.

questions.prompt: Why is `list.append` amortized O(1) even though an occasional append has to copy the whole list?
options: Append never copies; it only moves the end pointer
The capacity grows by a fixed number of slots each time, so copies are rare
CPython stores the list as a linked list, so there is nothing to copy
The capacity grows by a constant factor, so the total copying across n appends is O(n)
questions.explanation: When the array is full CPython allocates a larger one, growing proportionally to the current size, and copies the elements. Those copies form a geometric series (1 + 2 + 4 + ...) whose sum is O(n) over n appends, i.e. O(1) each on average. If capacity grew by a fixed number of slots, copies would happen every c appends and the total would be O(n²). A Python list is an array of references, not a linked list.

questions.prompt: Which operation is O(n) on a list but O(1) on a collections.deque?
options: Appending to the end
Removing the first element (`lst.pop(0)` vs `dq.popleft()`)
Reading the last element with [-1]
Checking len()
questions.explanation: A list is a contiguous array, so removing index 0 shifts every other element left: O(n). A deque is a doubly linked list of blocks, so popleft is O(1). Use a deque for queues and BFS. Appending at the end, [-1] and len() are O(1) on both (append is amortized).

questions.prompt: Let f(n) = 3n² + 5n + 7. Which statement is correct?
options: f(n) is Θ(n²), and it is also O(n³)
f(n) is O(n²) only; saying O(n³) is false
f(n) is Θ(n³)
f(n) is Ω(n³)
questions.explanation: Big-O is an upper bound, so any larger growth rate is also a valid (if loose) bound: f is O(n²) and O(n³). Θ(n²) says the bound is tight, which holds because the n² term dominates. Θ(n³) and Ω(n³) would claim f grows at least as fast as n³, which is false. In interviews, state the tight bound.

drill.description: Given a string, find the length of the longest substring that contains no repeated characters.
Reverse an array in place by swapping elements from both ends, moving toward the middle.
Count the number of contiguous subarrays whose elements add up to exactly k, in a single pass.
Return all elements of an m×n matrix in spiral order, starting from the top-left corner.
